Voice AI is ready to talk to customers. The harder question is: how would you know it is safe, helpful and worth the cost? This is what we found when we put it to the test.

We built an independent test environment, a simulated bank and simulated customers, and ran six selected external prototype services through it: OpenAI GPT-Realtime, OpenAI GPT-Live, Google Gemini Live, xAI Grok Voice, ElevenLabs Agents and Amazon Nova Sonic. These were tested outside of work, all on the same standardised prompt, apart from an adapter wrapper that GPT-Live also receives. In total: forty customer situations, repeated three times each, seven hundred and twenty recorded runs. One of those runs failed, and I will come back to it.

Every service faced the same situations, the same bank and the same scoring rules. Controls sit outside the service, holding speech back until policy allows it, and every run is written to a tamper-evident evidence ledger. If evidence is missing, that counts against the result. It is never quietly treated as a pass.

The first finding is protection. In seven hundred and twenty runs, no service carried out a prohibited action. That is the result of the services and the controls working together. It does not mean every check passed, and the report records the failures too, including one GPT-Realtime reply that ran past the audio limit and was stopped by the safety gate.

The second finding is that getting the job done varied. When a customer asked the bank to do something, four services completed all thirty-six eligible requests: xAI, ElevenLabs, Gemini and GPT-Realtime. Nova completed thirty-two, and GPT-Live twenty-nine.

Saying the right thing held up. A hundred and thirteen of a hundred and fourteen spoken-fact checks, such as amounts and dates, passed. The other was untestable because the spoken amount was ambiguous. None was wrong. Overall quality for the five services that could be scored sat between ninety-eight point nine and ninety-nine point six percent, and the statistics cannot separate them, so there is no clear overall winner. GPT-Realtime has no overall score because of its failed run.

Cost varied the most. The median voice cost per priced run ran from four tenths of a cent, for Gemini, to three point two cents, for xAI. That is roughly an eight times spread, for services that scored close together on the quality score. This covers voice usage only, and GPT-Live is billed by session time, so its figure is not like for like.

Across the baseline and five caller-voice batches, eighteen runs per service, a caller asks for a person and then asks again. GPT-Realtime, xAI and ElevenLabs transferred every time, and Gemini seventeen times. Nova did so eleven times in eighteen, and GPT-Live never did, offering to help with the account instead. A confirmed cancellation was completed every time by five services. Nova completed seventeen of eighteen, so the earlier zero-of-three did not repeat at that rate, though one run still failed. Fifteen of the eighteen sit outside the main scores, and the samples are small, but they are a reminder that handing over to a person needs testing too.

Two lessons stood out. First, a reply that sounds successful is not proof the bank action actually happened, so the test checks the action itself. Second, in earlier runs from the twenty-eighth to the thirtieth of October, broad prompt tuning moved individual results but not the overall ranking, while a couple of targeted prompt lines fixed specific failures, like Nova's handover to a person, in a small three-run diagnostic. The third of November run used one standard prompt throughout.

What this does not tell you matters. The callers are scripted and synthetic. Simulated street noise and a phone-line profile were tested, and a small exploratory test used four accent voices. Real customers and real-world noise were not. Customer care was not judged in the run itself, and a later check with two AI judges disagreed, so it remains unresolved. Samples are small. This is not a prediction of customer outcomes, not a certification, and it has not yet measured the services you already run, such as Amazon Connect or our internal agentic platforms. It is evidence about specific prototype configurations, on a specific day.

So what? Services that look the same on quality can differ sharply on completion and cost, and none of this shows up in a demo. The next step is to bring the harness inside the work environment, and baseline what we already run, Amazon Connect and our internal agentic platforms, against these prototypes. Pick the customer journey where a missed request or an unsafe action would hurt most. Define what helpful, protected and understandable mean for it. Then compare real experiences, on the same evidence, before anything new speaks to a customer.
